Sorry, what we see here is the wealthy class acting without impunity, which is the sad state of affairs as of this writing.

records.title: The Reading Room
records.comment:
This is a poignant and heart-warming story about a young girl who finally finds a place she belongs and finds peace.  

Laramia ran away from home at 15 to a shelter since she was born with a disease and shunned by her parents her entire life.  She survived by working various jobs all the while undergoing treatment.

She worked various jobs until she was able to rent a room above the garage of an old librarian who had cancer.  Manuela befriended Laramia and soon learned she was easily hired for jobs but was always terminated when the employer found out about her virus.  Manuela told Laramia to go to Heller Library and ask Gregoria for a job working in the stacks.  Once there, she met Icarus who showed her around the library, a place Laramia instantly felt at home and at ease.  As they approached the archive room where the library needed help, she was assigned to help the lead archivist with a new project.  

Icarus then leaned toward and whispered to Laramia that it didn’t matter what her disease was, that she’d be looked after.  She was finally home.

Ferris Bueller's Day Off: 40th Anniversary and Review
records.comment:
While I appreciate Jackson LeJeune's thoughtful review of Ferris
Bueller's Day Off, I think his perspective illustrates exactly why some
films can be difficult to fully understand when viewed outside the cultural
context in which they were created.

Ferris Bueller was never intended to be a moral role model. That's where I
believe younger viewers often miss the point. In 1986, Ferris represented
something far larger than a teenager skipping school. He embodied freedom,
spontaneity, and a rebellion against the increasingly structured,
achievement-driven culture that many young people felt trapped in. Ferris
wasn't admired because he was perfect; he was admired because he dared to
live in the moment.

The criticism that Ferris is selfish, privileged, and never faces
consequences is certainly valid if viewed through a modern lens. But
audiences in the 1980s weren't watching a cautionary tale. They were
watching a fantasy. Ferris was the kid who got away with what everyone else
only dreamed about. Just as Bugs Bunny isn't judged by modern workplace
ethics, Ferris wasn't intended to be evaluated by contemporary standards of
accountability.

What also gets overlooked is that Ferris's influence on Cameron is the
emotional heart of the film. Jackson correctly identifies Cameron as the
character who experiences the true arc, but Ferris's role is to serve as
the catalyst. Cameron begins the film paralyzed by fear, anxiety, and his
father's expectations. By the end, he is finally willing to confront his
reality. Without Ferris, that transformation never happens.

The article also criticizes the adults as cartoonish caricatures. Again,
that's by design. John Hughes deliberately tells the story from the
perspective of teenagers. To many teenagers, adults often seem oblivious,
disconnected, and obsessed with rules. The exaggerated portrayal isn't a
flaw; it's part of the film's comedic language.

Most importantly, Ferris Bueller captured the spirit of an era. For those
of us who actually lived through the 1970s and 1980s, life wasn't filtered
through smartphones, social media, GPS tracking, and constant connectivity.
A teenager could disappear for a day, explore a city, make memories with
friends, and return home with nothing but stories. That sense of freedom is
almost impossible to explain to someone who didn't experience it firsthand.

The film's famous message—"Life moves pretty fast. If you don't stop and
look around once in a while, you could miss it."—isn't an endorsement of
irresponsibility. It's a reminder not to become so consumed by obligations,
schedules, and expectations that you forget to actually live.

Forty years later, that's exactly why Ferris Bueller's Day Off remains
beloved. It isn't because Ferris is perfect. It's because, for one glorious
day, he reminds us what freedom feels like.
